a: About children
p: Codex Vaticanus gives some sections short titles, such as 'About children' here and 'About food' at 30:16.
b: The Greek text that Swete prints from Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) has short titles written into the text: Peri teknōn, "About children," here, and Peri brōmatōn, "About food," at 30:16. Swete's notes show that scribes added more: a corrector of B wrote a title "about health" between the lines at 30:14 and marked the one at 30:16 as wrong, Codex Ephraemi (C) adds "about slaves" in the margin at 30:33, and a hand in B writes "about leaders" beside 35:1. They were reading aids, like the headings in a modern Bible, not words of Ben Sira. The Plain keeps the two that stand in Swete's text, because it translates that text.

a: will keep the whip on him
t: Compared with the Bible: the rod
p: Ben Sira's hard line on beating sons goes further than Proverbs in detail, but not in principle.
b: Agrees with Proverbs: "Whoever keeps back his rod hates his son" (Proverbs 13:24), and "When you hit him with the rod, he will not die" (Proverbs 23:13). Goes beyond in its detail: "Bruise his ribs" (30:12), with no word of the father's restraint. The New Testament keeps discipline but adds a check on the father: "Fathers, do not stir your children to anger" (Ephesians 6:4), and Hebrews reads God's own discipline as a sign of love that "hands back a peaceful fruit" (Hebrews 12:11). Catholic and Orthodox readers, for whom the book is Scripture, read it as the wisdom of its time about firm training, set beside the Gospel's gentleness; Protestants, who read it as wisdom but not as Scripture, use it in the same way. Most modern readers of every tradition do not take 30:12 as a rule for today.

a: it is as if he had not died
p: Ben Sira's comfort at death is a son like his father, not a life after death.
b: For Ben Sira a man lives on in a son who is "like himself." The book nowhere promises the righteous a resurrection: the dead in Hades cannot praise God (17:27), and a man's name and children are what remain (compare 44:9–15). Historical-critical scholars see here the older Israelite hope, before the belief in resurrection of Daniel 12:2 spread. Catholic and Orthodox readers, for whom the book is Scripture, read it as an early stage of revelation that later Scripture fills out (Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7:9). See the note at 30:17.

a: Over his sons' lives he will be binding up wounds
p: The Greek reads 'for the lives of sons'; the same letters could be one word, 'coddling'.
b: Swete's text reads peri psychōn huiōn, "for the lives of sons," and the Latin, made from the Greek, reads the same (pro animabus filiorum). The Plain follows it: a father who spoils his sons will spend his life bandaging their hurts and churning at every cry. The old manuscripts were written without spaces, and the letters ΠΕΡΙΨΥΧΩΝ can also be read as one word, peripsychōn, "cherishing, coddling." That reading gives the sense of the KJV, "He that maketh too much of his son," and fits the next verses on the untamed horse and the pampered child. Sinaiticus as corrected and Alexandrinus have "son" in the singular. The point is the same either way: indulgence now means wounds later.

a: your own teeth will be set on edge
p: The image is the sour taste of regret, as in the proverb about sour grapes.
b: The verb gomphiazō means to have one's teeth set on edge, the numb, sour feeling of biting something unripe. Jeremiah and Ezekiel quote a proverb with the same picture: "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb" (Jeremiah 31:29). There the children pay for the parents; here the indulgent parent pays for his own laughter.
orig: γομφιάσεις τοὺς ὀδόντας σου (gomphiaseis tous odontas sou)

a: scourged in his own body
p: The Greek uses the word for flogging for a body racked by disease.
b: Memastigōmenos means "flogged, scourged," the word used of the whip in 30:1. The same picture of sickness as a lash appears in the Gospels, where a long illness is a mastix, a scourge (Mark 5:29, 34). Ben Sira turns the father's whip of 30:1 into the whip of illness: a rich man in pain is worse off than a poor man in good health.

a: Death is better than a bitter life
t: Compared with the Bible: is death better?
p: Job, Jeremiah and Ecclesiastes also wish for death in misery; the hope of resurrection is absent here.
b: Agrees with the Bible's honest laments: Job curses the day he was born (Job 3:1–26), Jeremiah too (Jeremiah 20:14–18), and Ecclesiastes praises the dead above the living (Ecclesiastes 4:2). Ben Sira speaks as a teacher, not as one in pain: a lasting sickness or a bitter life is worse than death. A corrector of Sinaiticus, the Hebrew and the Latin add "eternal rest" (see the variant). Goes beyond nothing the Bible says, but it stops short of the New Testament, where death is an enemy to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26) and the dead in Christ wait for resurrection.

a: laid out on a grave
p: Meals and food gifts for the dead were common in the ancient world; Ben Sira uses the custom as a picture of waste.
b: Many peoples around Israel left food and drink at tombs for the dead. The Law has a worshiper declare at the tithe, "I have not given any of it for the dead" (Deuteronomy 26:14), and Tobit tells his son to "pour out" his bread on the grave of the righteous (Tobit 4:17, read in more than one way). Ben Sira does not argue about the custom; he uses it as a picture: rich food set before a sick man who cannot eat is as useless as a meal on a grave. The next verse adds the idol that cannot eat.

a: What good is an offering to an idol?
p: Psalm 115 and the stories of Bel mock idols that cannot eat or smell.
b: The Psalms mock idols: "a nose they have, but they cannot smell" (Psalm 115:6), and Deuteronomy warns of gods "which cannot see or hear or eat or smell" (Deuteronomy 4:28). In Bel and the Dragon, one of the Greek additions to Daniel, the priests of Bel secretly eat the food set before the idol. Ben Sira's point is about the sick man: he is like an idol at its feast, surrounded by food he cannot enjoy. The Greek word karpōsis is a Septuagint word for an offering burned on the altar.

a: the one whom the Lord is hounding
p: The Greek calls the sick man one 'hunted by the Lord'; the Hebrew speaks of a rich man who cannot enjoy his wealth.
b: The Greek ekdiōkomenos hypo Kyriou means "pursued, hunted down by the Lord." It assumes the common belief that long illness is God's doing, the view Job's friends hold and the book of Job questions (Job 4:7–9; Job 42:7), and that Jesus sets aside for the man born blind (John 9:2–3). The Hebrew (see the variant) has a different line: a man with riches who gets no pleasure from them, a theme Ecclesiastes knows (Ecclesiastes 6:1–2). Readers should not build a doctrine of sickness on the Greek alone.

a: like a eunuch who holds a young woman in his arms
p: Ben Sira uses the same picture at 20:4, and a corrector of Vaticanus brought that line in here.
b: The picture is of desire that cannot be fulfilled: the sick man sees the food, as a eunuch holds a young woman, and can only groan. Ben Sira uses the same image at 20:4, where it ends, "so is the one who does justice by force." A later hand in Codex Vaticanus wrote that same line in the margin here, and the Hebrew in Kahana's edition has it too, so in some copies the picture applies both to the sick and to the unjust judge. On eunuchs in the Bible see Isaiah 56:3–5 and Acts 8:27.

a: Love yourself
p: The Greek says 'love your soul'; the Hebrew says 'refresh your soul'. It means, take care of yourself.
b: The Greek agapa tēn psychēn sou is literally "love your soul." In Hebrew and in the Greek of the Septuagint the "soul" is often simply the self. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has a different verb, "cheer, refresh yourself." Ben Sira is not teaching self-love against love of neighbor; he means, look after yourself and do not let grief eat you up. Read with 30:21–24 it is advice for the mind's health.
orig: ἀγάπα τὴν ψυχήν σου (agapa tēn psychēn sou)

a: for grief has killed many
p: The Talmud quotes a Ben Sira saying close to this one, among the parts of the book it says may be taught.
b: The Babylonian Talmud discusses Ben Sira in tractate Sanhedrin 100b. Among his sayings it weighs is one close to this verse: do not let worry into your heart, for worry has killed many strong men. The rabbis note that Solomon already said something like it (Proverbs 12:25). In the same passage Rav Yosef says that the good things in the book may be taught in public, although the book was not to be read as Scripture. So Ben Sira's advice on grief was still being repeated by Jewish teachers centuries after the book was set aside from the Hebrew Bible.

a: A bright and good heart
p: This verse holds two lines; the second is KJV 30:25. After it, the Greek and the Hebrew order part ways.
b: Swete's 30:24 holds two lines. The first is KJV 30:24 ("Envy and wrath shorten the life"); the second, "A bright and good heart," is KJV 30:25, the last verse of chapter 30 in the KJV. The digital Greek text has a stray bracketed number "[13]" between the two lines, which the Plain leaves out. Then the Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew and Latin go different ways. In the Greek, 30:25–40 comes next, which the KJV prints as 33:16–31. The KJV's 30:25 to 33:15 stands in the Greek, and on this site, as 34:1 to 36:15. Ben Sira's grandson's Greek was copied with two long blocks in swapped order, which scholars usually explain as sheets of an early copy put back in the wrong order. The Greek manuscripts all have this order, and Rahlfs, the Göttingen edition, Orthodox Bibles and this site keep the Greek numbers. The book's opening pages give the full table.

a: Like a gleaner behind the grape pickers
p: Verses 30:25–40 here are 33:16–31 in the KJV and most English Bibles; this verse begins in the middle of a sentence.
b: This verse is KJV 33:16 (second half), and 30:26–40 here are KJV 33:17–31 (KJV 33:27 is split over 30:36–37, and 30:38 holds KJV 33:28–29). In the Greek manuscripts the sentence has lost its start: "I too kept watch, the last of all" (KJV 33:16a) stands at 36:16, far away, where the two swapped blocks meet. Swete marks the break with a sign. So Ben Sira's words about himself read, in the Hebrew and Latin order: "I too kept watch, the last of all, like a gleaner behind the grape pickers." See the note at 30:24.

a: Like a gleaner
p: Ben Sira pictures himself as one who comes after the harvest of earlier sages, and still fills a winepress.
b: Gleaners gathered what the harvesters left (Leviticus 19:9–10; Ruth 2:2–3); after a grape harvest only scraps remain (Isaiah 24:13; Micah 7:1). Ben Sira says he came last, after the great teachers of Israel, yet by the Lord's blessing his gleaning filled a whole winepress. Scholars read it as a scribe's modest claim: he gathers and passes on the wisdom of those before him (compare 39:1–3). He makes the same claim of hard work for others at 24:34.

a: you leaders of the assembly
p: He turns to the great men of the people and the leaders of the assembly, the elite of Jerusalem.
b: The "great men" (megistanes) and "those who lead the assembly" (ekklēsia, the gathered people of Israel) are the leading families of Jerusalem in the early 100s BC, when Judea was passing from Ptolemaic to Seleucid rule. Ben Sira taught their sons (51:23) and sat among their counselors (39:4). The advice that follows, on keeping control of property and managing slaves, is advice for men with estates and households.

a: Do not give your property to someone else
t: The father who divided his living
p: Ben Sira warns against what the father in Jesus' parable does: hand over his property while he lives.
b: In the parable of the lost son the younger son says, "Father, give me the part of the estate that falls to me," and the father divides his living between his sons (Luke 15:12). Ben Sira's advice is the opposite: keep your property under your hand until your dying day (30:32), or you may end up begging your own children. Read beside this verse, the father in the parable is shown to be generous beyond prudence, which fits the parable's picture of God.

a: your glory
p: Doxa here is a man's honor and reputation.
b: Doxa is "glory," the word used for God's glory. Of a person it means honor, standing, reputation: what others think of you. In an honor-based society a father who lost control of his household lost his doxa. The Plain keeps "glory" as this book's term.
orig: ἐν τῇ δόξῃ σου (en tē doxē sou)

a: a slave
p: Ben Sira's oiketēs is a slave of the household; the KJV's 'servant' hides that.
b: Oiketēs is a household slave, and pais in 30:34 is the ordinary word for a young slave. The KJV says "servant," as many English Bibles do, but these were people bought and owned (30:39 "you got him"). Slaves in Judea in Ben Sira's time included Jews sold for debt, whom the Law said must go free in the seventh year (Deuteronomy 15:12), and foreigners bought or taken in war. Ben Sira's readers were slave owners, and he writes for them.

a: the rack and torture
t: Compared with the Bible: harsh masters
p: Ben Sira allows torture of a bad slave; the Law limits a master's violence, and the New Testament tells masters to be just.
b: Goes beyond the Law in harshness. The Law does not forbid slavery, but it limits it: a slave who loses an eye or a tooth by his master's blow goes free (Exodus 21:26–27), a master who kills a slave is punished (Exodus 21:20), and a Hebrew slave goes free in the seventh year (Deuteronomy 15:12). Ben Sira's racks and fetters (30:38) are not in the Law. He then turns: "do not go too far," treat the slave "like yourself" (30:38–39). Job had said that one Maker shaped master and slave alike (Job 31:15), and Paul tells masters to give slaves "what is just and what is equal" (Colossians 4:1). Readers in every church today read 30:33–38 as a record of the slave-owning world, not as a model.
r: Exodus 21:20; Exodus 21:26–27; Deuteronomy 15:12; Job 31:13–15; Colossians 4:1; Ephesians 6:9

a: at the cost of blood
p: The Greek says 'in blood you acquired him'; the KJV says 'bought with a price'.
b: En haimati ektēsō auton, "in blood you acquired him." Readers take it in two ways: (1) at great cost, money earned with your life's sweat, as the Latin seems to read it ("with the blood of the soul"); (2) by bloodshed, a captive taken in war. The KJV's "bought him with a price" gives the first sense. Either way the point is that a slave is costly and worth keeping, and the verse moves from self-interest toward something more: "let him be like yourself."
orig: ἐν αἵματι ἐκτήσω αὐτόν (en haimati ektēsō auton)

a: you need him as you need your own life
t: Compared with the Bible: the slave as yourself
p: Ben Sira's 'treat him like yourself' echoes the command to love one's neighbor, and points toward Philemon.
b: Agrees with the Law's "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18) and with Job, who feared to wrong his slaves because God made them too (Job 31:13–15). Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "treat him like a brother" (see the variant), which Paul goes beyond when he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 1:16). Ben Sira's reason is partly practical (you need him, 30:40), but the words lean toward the equality the New Testament states.

a: A man without sense has empty and false hopes
p: This chapter is chapter 34 in the KJV and most English Bibles.
b: Chapter 31 here is KJV 34 (its 31 verses hold KJV 34:1–26; KJV 34:10, 13, 15, 18 and 22 are each split over two Greek verses). It belongs to the long block that the Greek manuscripts put before chapters 34–36 (see the note at 30:24). English Bibles that follow the Hebrew and Latin order, such as the KJV and most modern Catholic and Protestant Bibles, call this chapter 34; Orthodox Bibles and editions of the Greek call it 31.

a: dreams give fools wings
p: The Bible records dreams sent by God and warns against dreamers; Ben Sira keeps both.
b: Agrees. The Bible has dreams sent by God, to Joseph (Genesis 37:5), to Pharaoh, to Nebuchadnezzar through Daniel (Daniel 2:28) and to Joseph in Matthew (Matthew 1:20); the LORD says he speaks to a prophet "in a dream" (Numbers 12:6). It also warns against "that dreamer of dreams" who leads to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:3), and Jeremiah sets a dream against the LORD's word: "What has straw got to do with grain?" (Jeremiah 23:28). Ecclesiastes: "where dreams are many, there are vapors" (Ecclesiastes 5:7). Ben Sira holds the same line: dreams are empty unless the Most High sends them (31:6), and the sure guide is the law (31:8).
r: Genesis 37:5; Daniel 2:28; Matthew 1:20; Numbers 12:6; Deuteronomy 13:1–3; Jeremiah 23:25–28; Ecclesiastes 5:7; Zechariah 10:2; 31:6; 31:8

a: chasing the wind
p: Ecclesiastes uses the same picture for what comes to nothing.
b: Ecclesiastes says that all that is done under the sun is "vapor and chasing the wind" (Ecclesiastes 1:14), and Hosea says Ephraim "runs after the scorching east wind" (Hosea 12:1). Ben Sira puts dreams with the shadow and the wind: things you can see but never hold.

a: the likeness of a face before a face
p: A dream only shows you your own face, as in a mirror or in water.
b: "This against that" and "a face before a face" picture a reflection. A dream shows a likeness, not the thing itself, and often what it shows is the dreamer's own hopes looking back at him. Proverbs uses the picture of water that reflects a face (Proverbs 27:19), and Paul says that now we "look through a mirror" (1 Corinthians 13:12).

a: What can be made clean by something unclean?
p: Job asks the same question about human nature.
b: Job asks, "Who can make what is clean come out of what is unclean? / No one can" (Job 14:4). Ben Sira uses the same question for knowledge: a false source cannot give a true answer. The purity language prepares for 31:30, where a man washes after touching a corpse and then touches it again.

a: Divination, omens and dreams are all empty
p: The Law forbids divination and omen-reading; Ben Sira puts dreams in the same group.
b: Manteiai (divination) and oiōnismoi (reading omens, for example from the flight of birds) are the practices the Law forbids: "anyone who practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens" (Deuteronomy 18:10). In the Greek cities of Ben Sira's day dream interpreters and oracles were a trade. The comparison with a woman in labor is of the fevered fancies of pain: the heart sees what it fears or wants.

a: as a visit from him
p: Episkopē, 'visitation', is a time when God comes near to act.
b: En episkopē, "in a visitation." In the Septuagint God's "visit" is a time when he comes to act, to save or to judge (Genesis 50:24 in Greek; Luke 1:68; Luke 19:44). Ben Sira allows that a dream may be such a visit; he just warns that most are not. The word episkopos, "overseer," comes from the same root.

a: Without any lie the law will be fulfilled
p: Against unreliable dreams Ben Sira sets the law, which will be carried out to the full.
b: The verb syntelesthēsetai means "will be completed, carried out to the end." Ben Sira's point: you do not need dreams to know God's will; the law of Moses is sure. Jesus says, "not one iota or one tiny hook of a letter will ever drop out of the Law, until all things have come about" (Matthew 5:18). The link between dreams and the law is Deuteronomy 13, where a dreamer who leads away from the commands must not be heard.

a: A well-taught man
p: Ben Sira praises learning from travel, a mark of the scribe who served rulers abroad.
b: In 39:4 Ben Sira says the scribe serves among great men and passes through the lands of foreign nations, testing good and evil among people. Wealthy Jews of his time served the Ptolemies and Seleucids as envoys and officials, and a scribe might travel with them. Here he speaks of himself (31:12–13): he has seen much and been in danger. Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "a man who has traveled" instead of "a well-taught man" (see the variant), which fits the next verses.

a: grow rich in shrewdness
p: Panourgia is usually 'cunning', but here it is the good shrewdness of experience.
b: Panourgia often means craftiness, as in Luke 20:23. In Proverbs the Greek uses it for the good "shrewdness" a young man needs (Proverbs 1:4; 8:5). Here it is the good kind: the know-how of someone who has seen the world. The Plain uses "shrewdness," the word this site uses for the Proverbs term, so the link shows.

a: I have seen much in my wanderings
p: One of the few places where Ben Sira speaks of his own life.
b: Ben Sira rarely speaks of himself; here and at 51:1–12 he does. He traveled, saw much, and was often near death (31:13). The book does not say where he went. Scholars have suggested service with a Jerusalem embassy or a ruler's court, but that is a guess. Job had asked his friends to listen to "people passing along the road" (Job 21:29); Ben Sira is such a traveler, and his travels taught him to trust the Lord (31:14–20).

a: because of these things
t: 'Because of these' or 'by the grace of God'?
p: The Greek says he was saved 'because of these things'; the Latin turned charin into 'by the grace of God'.
b: The Greek toutōn charin means "for the sake of these things, because of these." Charin used this way is a preposition, but it is also the word for "grace." The Latin reads liberatus sum gratia Dei, "I was set free by the grace of God," and the Douay-Rheims follows. What "these things" are is left open: the lessons of travel, or the fear of the Lord in the next verses.

a: The Lord keeps his eyes on those who love him
p: The Psalms picture the Lord's eyes on those who fear him, and the Lord as shade from the heat.
b: "Look: the LORD's eye is toward those who fear him" (Psalm 33:18); "The LORD's eyes turn toward the righteous" (Psalm 34:15). The shade from burning heat and the noon sun are the pictures of Psalm 121:5–6 and Isaiah 25:4, "a shade from the heat." The guard against stumbling recalls Psalm 121:3, "May he never let your foot slide."

a: A sacrifice from ill-gotten goods
p: In 1514 Bartolomé de las Casas read this passage and gave up his slaves in the Americas.
b: The Spanish priest and settler Bartolomé de las Casas held an encomienda, a grant of the labor of native people, in Spain's new colonies in the Americas. In 1514, while preparing a Pentecost sermon on this passage (Ecclesiasticus 34:18–22 in the Latin and KJV numbering, 31:21–27 here), he became convinced that the Spaniards' treatment of the native peoples was unjust. He gave up his slaves and his grant and spent the rest of his life defending the native peoples. Few passages of a book outside the Hebrew Bible have changed a life so plainly.

a: does not make atonement for sins
t: Compared with the Bible: sacrifice without justice
p: Ben Sira repeats the prophets: God does not accept sacrifice from those who wrong the poor.
b: Agrees with the prophets and Proverbs: "When the wicked sacrifice, the LORD finds it abhorrent" (Proverbs 15:8); "What use to me are all your many sacrifices?" (Isaiah 1:11); "I will not be pleased with them" (Amos 5:22). Ben Sira was no critic of the temple: he loved its worship (50:1–21) and tells his readers to bring offerings (32:6–11). His point is the prophets' point: an offering paid for by injustice is a mockery (31:21). Jesus tells a worshiper to be reconciled with his brother before bringing his gift (Matthew 5:23–24).

a: Killing a son in front of his father
p: To sacrifice from the poor man's goods is as monstrous as killing a son before his father's eyes.
b: The picture is shocking on purpose. The poor man's goods are his children's food (31:25); to make an offering from them is to kill in front of a father what he loves most. The Hebrew Bible links bloodshed and false worship in the same way ("Blood fills your hands," Isaiah 1:15).

a: a man of blood
p: A Hebrew way of saying 'murderer'.
b: Anthrōpos haimatōn, "a man of bloods," is a Hebrew idiom for a murderer (2 Samuel 16:7–8, of David in Shimei's curse; Psalm 5:6). Ben Sira calls the one who takes the poor man's bread a murderer, because bread is the poor man's life. 31:26–27 repeat the point for wages.

a: holds back a hired man's pay
p: The Law, the prophets and James condemn holding back a worker's pay.
b: "The wages of a hired worker must not stay with you overnight" (Leviticus 19:13); "Pay him his wages each day... Otherwise he will cry out to the LORD against you" (Deuteronomy 24:15). Malachi names those who cheat the hired man (Malachi 3:5), and James writes, "The pay of the laborers... the pay you cheated them out of, cries out" (James 5:4). Tobit tells his son the same (Tobit 4:14). Ben Sira calls it shedding blood.

a: which voice will the Master hear?
p: Despotēs is 'Master', a title of God in the Greek books.
b: Ho despotēs, "the Master," is a title for God in the Greek books, as in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees, and in the prayer of Acts 4:24. This site keeps "Master" for it, apart from Kyrios, "the Lord." The prayer in chapter 33 begins with the same title (33:1).

a: A man bathes after contact with a dead body
p: The Law made anyone who touched a dead body unclean for seven days, to be cleansed with water.
b: Under the Law, "Whoever touches a dead body... will be unclean seven days" and must be cleansed on the third and seventh days with the water of the red heifer's ashes (Numbers 19:11–12). The Greek verb is baptizomenos, "being dipped, washed," the word later used for baptism; here it is a plain ritual bath. Ben Sira's point: a bath is useless if you go straight back to the corpse.

a: what good was his bath?
p: The Talmud uses the same picture: a man who confesses but keeps his sin is like one who bathes holding something unclean.
b: The Babylonian Talmud (Taanit 16a) gives a saying of Rav Adda bar Ahava: a person who confesses a sin but does not turn from it is like someone who holds a dead creeping thing, a source of uncleanness, in his hand. Even if he bathed in all the waters of the world, his bath would not help; once he throws it away, one bath is enough. The rabbis support it with Proverbs 28:13. It is Ben Sira's picture of 31:30–31, kept in Jewish teaching centuries later.

a: fasts for his sins
t: Compared with the Bible: fasting without change
p: The prophets and the New Testament say the same: repentance must change what we do.
b: Agrees. Isaiah: "Is this not the fasting I choose: / to unlock the fetters of wickedness" (Isaiah 58:6). Proverbs: "A dog goes back to its vomit, / and a fool does his folly over again" (Proverbs 26:11), which 2 Peter 2:22 applies to those who turn back after knowing the way. Ben Sira assumes, as Jewish teaching of his time did, that fasting and prayer can win forgiveness, but only with a changed life. Catholic and Orthodox readers, who keep fasts of repentance, read the verse as the condition of a true fast; Protestants read it the same way.

a: Whoever keeps the law brings offerings in plenty
p: This chapter is chapter 35 in the KJV and most English Bibles.
b: Chapter 32 here is KJV 35:1–20 (KJV 35:1, 2, 12, 15, 17 and 19 are each split over two Greek verses; 32:22 holds the end of KJV 35:17 and the start of 35:18). English Bibles in the Hebrew and Latin order call it chapter 35. Notes in this site's books on Luke and Romans cite it as Sirach 32 (see the note at 30:24).

a: offers a peace offering
p: Thysia sōtēriou is the Septuagint's name for the shelamim, the peace offering.
b: The Greek thysiazōn sōtēriou, "sacrificing of salvation," uses the Septuagint's term for the Hebrew shelamim, the peace offering shared by the worshiper, the priest and God (Leviticus 3; Leviticus 7:11–18). Ben Sira matches each kind of good deed with a kind of offering: keeping the law with many offerings, attention to the commandments with a peace offering, repaying a kindness with fine flour (the grain offering of Leviticus 2:1), almsgiving with a sacrifice of praise.

a: whoever gives alms offers a sacrifice of praise
t: Compared with the Bible: deeds as sacrifices
p: Ben Sira calls obedience and alms sacrifices; Hebrews says the same of praise and sharing.
b: Agrees with the prophets and the New Testament. Samuel: "listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22); Hosea: "Loyal love is what I want, not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6). The "sacrifice of praise" is the Greek of Psalm 50:14 (49:14 in the Septuagint). Hebrews joins the two: "let us keep bringing up to God a sacrifice of praise," and "do not forget kindness and sharing. Those are the kinds of sacrifices God takes pleasure in" (Hebrews 13:15–16). Ben Sira still expects the temple offerings to be brought (32:6–11); the deeds do not replace them but give them meaning. Tobit 4:11 makes the same link for alms.
r: 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Psalm 50:14; Hebrews 13:15–16; Tobit 4:11; Philippians 4:18

a: makes atonement
t: Compared with the Bible: turning from sin as atonement
p: Ben Sira calls turning from wrong an atonement, as he called alms one at 3:30; churches read this differently.
b: The Greek exilasmos is the Septuagint word for atonement (the Day of Atonement is "the day of exilasmos," Leviticus 23:27 in Greek). Ben Sira says that turning from wrongdoing "makes atonement," as he said almsgiving does (3:30). Agrees with Ezekiel, who says the wicked who turns from sin will live (Ezekiel 18:21–22), and with Proverbs 16:6 in the Hebrew ("Guilt is atoned for by loyal love and faithfulness"). Catholic and Orthodox readers take it as teaching that repentance and good works have a real place in forgiveness, always by God's grace. Protestants read it as true of the old covenant's call to repent but not as a ground of forgiveness, which rests on Christ's atonement alone (Romans 3:24–25). Tobit's chapter 4 card on this site asks the same question for alms.

a: Do not appear before the Lord with empty hands
p: Ben Sira quotes the Law's rule for the pilgrim feasts.
b: The Law says three times: "No one is to appear before the LORD with empty hands" (Deuteronomy 16:16; compare Exodus 23:15; Exodus 34:20). Ben Sira cites it as a commandment (32:7): offerings are brought because God commanded them, not because God needs them. The Greek here follows the Septuagint wording of Exodus 23:15 closely (ouk ophthēsē... kenos).

a: its token portion will not be forgotten
p: Mnēmosynon is both a 'memorial' and the priest's token portion of a grain offering.
b: In the Greek of Leviticus the mnēmosynon is the handful of a grain offering that the priest burns on the altar as its "token portion" (Leviticus 2:2), the Hebrew azkarah, from the verb "remember." Ben Sira plays on both senses: God will not forget the token portion of a righteous man's sacrifice. Acts uses the same word for Cornelius: "your alms too, as a remembrance" (Acts 10:4).

a: with a good eye
p: A 'good eye' means generosity; an 'evil eye' means stinginess or envy.
b: In Hebrew and in the Greek of these books a "good eye" is a generous spirit, and an "evil eye" is a grudging, envious one (34:13). Proverbs: "The person with a kind eye will be blessed, / since he gives some of his bread to the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). Jesus uses the idiom: "is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15; compare Matthew 6:22–23).

a: let your face be glad
p: Paul's 'God loves a glad giver' uses a related word.
b: The verb hilarōson, "make glad," belongs with hilaros, "glad, cheerful," the word in "God loves a glad giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Paul's phrase is close to a line the Septuagint adds at Proverbs 22:8, "God blesses a glad man and a giver." Ben Sira gives the same advice for tithes and offerings: give with a glad face.

a: Give to the Most High in keeping with what he gives
t: Give as you have been given
p: Tobit and Deuteronomy say the same: give in proportion to what God has given you.
b: "Each of you is to bring what his hand can give, as the LORD your God has blessed you" (Deuteronomy 16:17). Tobit: "If you have plenty, give alms in keeping with your plenty" (Tobit 4:8). Paul asks each believer to set aside what he has earned (1 Corinthians 16:2). Ben Sira's "as far as your hand can reach" is literally "according to the finding of the hand," what you have been able to gain.

a: seven times over he will pay you back
t: Compared with the Bible: God repays
p: Ben Sira promises a sevenfold return; Proverbs and Jesus also speak of God's repayment.
b: Agrees in principle: "Showing kindness to a poor man is a loan made to the LORD, / and he will pay him back for what he did" (Proverbs 19:17); "Test me by doing this... will I not open the windows of the heavens for you" (Malachi 3:10); Jesus promises a hundredfold to those who leave all (Mark 10:29–30). The Hebrew in Kahana's edition adds a line close to Proverbs 19:17. Christians differ on how far such promises are about material gain: most traditions read them as God's faithfulness, not a formula for wealth.

a: Do not try to bribe him
p: Deuteronomy says God 'does not take a bribe'; Ben Sira applies it to sacrifice.
b: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Ben Sira draws the conclusion for worship: a sacrifice offered to buy God's favor, or to cover injustice (32:15), is a bribe, and God will not take it. Romans 2:11 and its note on this site cite this passage for God's impartiality.

a: no one's face wins special honor
p: 'Glory of face' and 'take a face' are Hebrew ways of saying favoritism.
b: Doxa prosōpou, "glory of face," and in 32:16 lēmpsetai prosōpon, "he will take a face," render the Hebrew idiom nasa panim, "lift the face," to favor someone for who they are. The New Testament coins a single word from it, prosōpolēmpsia, favoritism (Romans 2:11). God gives no weight to rank: not to the rich who can bring large offerings, and not, the next verse adds, against the poor.

a: nor a widow as she pours out her words
p: The Law warns that God hears the widow and the orphan; Jesus' parable of the widow builds on the same hope.
b: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly. / If you do treat him harshly, and he cries out to me, be sure I will hear his cry" (Exodus 22:22–23). God "sees that the orphan and the widow get justice" (Deuteronomy 10:18). Widows had no husband to speak for them in court, so they were easy to wrong. In Luke 18:1–8 a widow keeps coming to a crooked judge; Jesus argues that God, who is the opposite of that judge, will surely act. The notes on Luke 18 on this site point to this passage (32:14–22).

a: The prayer of the humble has gone through the clouds
p: A famous line: the prayer of the lowly rises past the clouds and does not rest until God acts.
b: Clouds stand between earth and God's throne ("You covered yourself with cloud, and no prayer gets through," Lamentations 3:44). Ben Sira says the humble man's prayer goes right through, and keeps pressing until God "looks into it": the picture of persistent prayer that Luke 18:1 gives as the point of the widow's parable. Revelation shows the prayers of the saints rising before God with the incense (Revelation 8:3–4). The Catholic lectionary reads this passage on the 30th Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C (there numbered Sirach 35:12–14, 16–18).

a: nor will he be patient with them
p: Luke 18:7 uses the same Greek phrase; here God will not be patient with the oppressors.
b: The Greek makrothymēsei ep' autois, "be patient over them," is the same phrase Jesus uses at the end of the widow's parable: kai makrothymei ep' autois (Luke 18:7). Luke 18:7 also speaks of God getting justice (ekdikēsis), as Sirach does in 32:23 ("vengeance"). Here "them" are the merciless oppressors: the Lord will not hold back from punishing them. In Luke the phrase is debated ("Is he slow to act for them?"), and one reading, given in the site's note there, takes it from this verse. The wording is the same; whether Jesus or Luke had Ben Sira in mind cannot be proved.
orig: οὐδὲ μὴ μακροθυμήσει ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς (oude mē makrothymēsei ep' autois)

a: pays the nations back with vengeance
p: From the widow's cry Ben Sira moves to the nations who oppress Israel, and so to the prayer of chapter 33.
b: The thought widens: the merciless man of 32:22 becomes the nations, the arrogant and the scepters of unjust rulers. In the Greek order this leads straight into the prayer for Israel (33:1–13). Historical-critical scholars hear the hard years of Judea between the Ptolemaic and Seleucid empires about 200 BC, when foreign armies crossed the land and foreign kings taxed it. Jewish and Christian readers have heard here the promise that God will judge the oppressors of his people (Psalm 94:1–7; Revelation 6:10).

a: until he pays each person back for what he has done
p: The Psalms and Paul say God repays each by what he has done.
b: "You pay each person back by what he does" (Psalm 62:12); Paul quotes it: "He will pay back each person according to his works" (Romans 2:6). Proverbs 24:12 and Revelation 22:12 say the same. Ben Sira adds that God judges intentions (enthymēmata) as well as deeds.

a: like rain clouds in a season of drought
p: In a land that depends on rain, mercy in trouble is like clouds after a dry spell.
b: Judea's crops depend on the winter rains. Clouds after a drought were the clearest picture of rescue (1 Kings 18:44–45; Proverbs 16:15, a king's goodwill "like a cloud heavy with the late rains"). The clouds that the humble man's prayer went through (32:21) come back as clouds of rain: the answer.

a: Have mercy on us
p: Verses 33:1–13 here are KJV 36:1–11a; the prayer breaks off at 33:13 and goes on at 36:16.
b: This prayer is KJV 36:1–17, but in the Greek order it is cut in two. Its first half stands here as 33:1–13 (= KJV 36:1–11a; KJV 36:1, 6 and 7 are each split over two Greek verses). Then come the chapters on wealth, banquets and the law (34:1–36:15 = KJV 31:1–33:15). The prayer picks up again at 36:16, which joins the end of one block to the start of the other, and 36:17–22 are KJV 36:12–17. The Catholic lectionary reads parts of the prayer on Wednesday of the 8th week in Ordinary Time, Year I (there numbered Sirach 36).

a: cast the fear of you
p: Ben Sira prays for God to strike the nations that rule Israel. Who were they?
b: The prayer asks God to raise his hand "over the foreign nations," crush the heads of hostile rulers (33:12) and gather Israel (33:13). Most historical-critical scholars date Ben Sira's book about 190–180 BC, when Judea had just passed from the Ptolemies of Egypt to the Seleucids of Syria, and read the prayer as aimed at those empires. Because its fierce tone differs from the rest of the book, some scholars have asked whether it was added later, in the persecution of the 160s BC; others answer that its themes (Zion, the tribes, Aaron's blessing) are Ben Sira's own. Jewish and Christian readers have used it as a prayer for God's rule over all nations, ending in 33:5: "that there is no God but you."

a: As you showed yourself holy through us in front of them
p: The words come from Ezekiel: God shows himself holy through Israel before the nations.
b: Ezekiel: "Then the nations will know that I am the LORD... when I show myself holy through you in front of them" (Ezekiel 36:23); and "So I will prove myself great and holy" (Ezekiel 38:23). When Israel was punished and scattered, the nations saw God's holiness in his judgment of his own people. Now Ben Sira asks for the reverse: let Israel see God's greatness shown in what he does to the nations.

a: that there is no God but you, Lord
p: The confession of Isaiah and of Solomon's prayer.
b: "There is no other god besides me" (Isaiah 45:21); Solomon prays "so that every people on earth will know that the LORD is God. There is no other" (1 Kings 8:60). Ben Sira asks that the nations come to know God "just as we have known," the hope that ends the prayer too (36:22).

a: Renew your signs
p: The Hebrew says 'renew a sign and repeat a wonder'; the Greek read the second verb as 'change'.
b: The Hebrew in Kahana's edition reads chaddesh ot ushneh mofet, "renew a sign and repeat a wonder." The Hebrew verb shanah can mean both "do again" and "change," and the Greek took it as alloiōson, "change, alter." The prayer asks for new acts like the signs and wonders of the exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; Psalm 77:14).
orig: ἐγκαίνισον σημεῖα καὶ ἀλλοίωσον θαυμάσια (enkainison sēmeia kai alloiōson thaumasia)

a: Give glory to your hand and your right arm
t: The hand and the right arm
p: The language of the Song of the Sea and the exodus.
b: "Your right hand, O LORD, / is splendid in strength" (Exodus 15:6); God brought Israel out "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 5:15). The prayer asks God to act again as at the exodus.

a: Take away the opponent
p: Antidikos is an opponent at law, the word the widow uses in Luke 18:3.
b: Antidikos means an opponent in a lawsuit, as in Luke 18:3, where the widow says "Defend my rights against my opponent at law." The prayer pictures Israel as a party in a case before God the judge, which links it with 32:14–25.

a: remember your oath
p: Remember the oath you swore to the fathers; the Hebrew says 'appoint the set time'.
b: The Greek horkismos is an "oath": God's sworn promise to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Genesis 22:16–18; Luke 1:73). The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has "hurry the end, appoint the set time, for who can say to you, 'What are you doing?'" (see the variant), the language of the end in Habakkuk and Daniel (Habakkuk 2:3; Daniel 8:19). The Latin reads "remember the end." The prayer asks God not to wait any longer.

a: Let the one who escapes be eaten up by fiery anger
t: Compared with the Bible: praying against enemies
p: Prayers for the enemy's ruin are in the Psalms too; Jesus teaches love of enemies.
b: Agrees with the Psalms of cursing (Psalm 79:6; Psalm 137:7–9) and the prophets' oracles against the nations, which ask God to punish those who crush his people. Conflicts, in spirit at least, with Jesus' "keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44), though the New Testament also has the martyrs' cry for justice (Revelation 6:10). Christians of every tradition who use this prayer read its curses, as they read the Psalms', as a cry to God for justice that leaves vengeance to him (Romans 12:19). Kahana's Hebrew has no line for this verse.

a: who say, "There is no one but us."
p: The boast of proud empires in Isaiah and Zephaniah.
b: Babylon says in its heart, "I am, and besides me there is nothing" (Isaiah 47:8), and so does Nineveh (Zephaniah 2:15). Ben Sira gives the same boast to the rulers of the nations. It is the reverse of Israel's confession in 33:5: there is no God but the Lord.

a: Gather all the tribes of Jacob
p: Ben Sira prays for all twelve tribes to be gathered; the sentence ends at 36:16.
b: Long after the northern tribes were scattered by Assyria, the prophets promised that God would gather "Israel's outcasts" and "Judah's scattered ones" (Isaiah 11:12) and set "the tribes of Jacob on their feet" (Isaiah 49:6). Ben Sira gives Elijah the task of restoring the tribes of Jacob (48:10). In the Hebrew the sentence goes on, "and let them take their inheritance as in days of old"; in the Greek order that half stands at 36:16. The New Testament takes up the hope: Jesus promises the Twelve that they will judge "the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matthew 19:28), and John says Jesus would die "to bring God's scattered children together into one" (John 11:52). Jewish daily prayer still asks God to gather the exiles.

a: Staying up nights over riches
p: Chapters 34–36:15 here are KJV 31:1–33:15.
b: Chapter 34 here is KJV 31 (the same verse numbers, 1–31). Chapter 35 here is KJV 32, and 36:1–15 here are KJV 33:1–15. In the Hebrew and Latin order these come right after chapter 30; in the Greek order they come after the block of 30:25–33:13. Notes on John 2 and Luke 15 on this site cite this block in the Greek numbers (see the note at 30:24).

a: he stuffs himself with his delicacies
p: Jesus' rich fool plans to rest, eat and drink; Ecclesiastes says the rich man's fullness spoils his sleep.
b: The rich man in Jesus' parable says to himself, "Rest now. Eat, drink, celebrate," and God calls him "Fool!" (Luke 12:19–20). Ecclesiastes: "A worker's sleep is sweet... But the rich man's fullness leaves him no rest to sleep" (Ecclesiastes 5:12). Ben Sira sets the rich and the poor side by side (34:3–4): both toil, but only the rich can rest, and even his rest is spoiled by worry (34:1).

a: Whoever loves gold will not be found in the right
p: The Greek verb is the one later used for 'justify'; here it means 'be held innocent'.
b: Ou dikaiōthēsetai, "will not be justified," uses the verb Paul makes famous (Romans 3:28). In Ben Sira, as in the Psalms (Psalm 143:2), it means to be found innocent at judgment. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has a related legal word, "will not go unpunished." Paul's "A root of every kind of evil is the love of money" (1 Timothy 6:10) says much the same.

a: those who sacrifice to it
p: Vaticanus reads 'those who sacrifice to it'; Sinaiticus first wrote 'those who are mad about it'.
b: Swete's text enthysiazousin means "those who sacrifice to it," making gold an idol; the KJV has the same, "them that sacrifice unto it." The first hand of Sinaiticus wrote enthousiazousin, "those who are possessed by it, mad about it" (see the variant). The Hebrew in Kahana's edition says only that it is a stumbling block "to the stubborn fool." The thought is close to Jesus' "You cannot be a slave both to God and to wealth" (Matthew 6:24) and to Paul's "greed is idolatry" (Colossians 3:5).
orig: ξύλον προσκόμματός ἐστιν τοῖς ἐνθυσιάζουσιν αὐτῷ (xylon proskommatos estin tois enthysiazousin autō)

a: who did not run after gold
p: The Hebrew here has mamon, 'wealth', the word Jesus uses in 'God and mammon'.
b: Where the Greek has "gold," the Hebrew in Kahana's edition reads mamon, "wealth, money": "and did not turn aside after mammon." This is one of the earliest uses of the word in Hebrew. Jesus uses it in Aramaic form, kept in the Greek of the Gospels as mamōnas: "You cannot be a slave both to God and to wealth" (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13). Ben Sira's blessing on the rich man who stayed blameless shows that he did not think wealth itself was evil, only the chase after it.

a: Blessed the rich man found with no blemish
t: Compared with the Bible: the righteous rich
p: Ben Sira thinks a blameless rich man is rare but possible; Jesus says it is hard, but possible with God.
b: Agrees with the Bible's mixed view of wealth. Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea are rich and righteous (Genesis 13:2; Job 1:1–3; Matthew 27:57). Proverbs prays for neither poverty nor riches (Proverbs 30:8–9). Jesus: "how hard it will be for the rich to enter God's kingdom," yet "With God, anything is possible" (Mark 10:27). Ben Sira's question, "Who is he?" (34:9), expects such a man to be rare, a marvel among his people.

a: the assembly will tell of his alms
t: Compared with the Bible: praise for giving
p: Ben Sira expects the assembly to praise a rich man's alms; Jesus tells givers to keep it secret.
b: Ben Sira's honest rich man will have his alms told in the ekklēsia, the gathered people. Generous donors in the Jewish and Greek world were often honored in public, with inscriptions or praise. Jesus warns against giving to be seen: "keep your left hand from knowing what your right hand does" (Matthew 6:2–3). The two need not conflict: Ben Sira describes the honor that follows, not the motive for giving. But the emphasis is different, and readers should notice it.

a: Are you seated at a great table?
p: Proverbs gives the same advice: control your appetite at a ruler's table.
b: "When you sit at a ruler's table to eat, / pay close attention to what is in front of you. / Put a knife to your throat / if you are a man of large appetite" (Proverbs 23:1–2). Ben Sira's "Do not open your throat wide" takes up the same picture. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition begins, "My son, if you sit at a great table." A young scribe who would serve great men had to know how to behave at their banquets.

a: an evil eye
p: An 'evil eye' here is greed at the table, not a magic curse.
b: In the ancient world the "evil eye" could mean a curse cast by an envious look, but in the Bible and in Ben Sira it means a grudging, greedy spirit: "is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15). At the table it is the eye that roams over every dish and wants it all. Ben Sira says no part of creation is greedier, and so the eye "weeps" at everything: it is never satisfied (compare Proverbs 27:20).

a: do not jostle him in the bowl
p: Diners dipped bread into a shared bowl; the same Greek word is used at the Last Supper.
b: At a meal several people dipped their bread into a common dish, the tryblion. Good manners meant not reaching for the piece your neighbor was eyeing and not pushing into the bowl with him. The same word appears at the Last Supper: "He is dipping into the same bowl as I am" (Mark 14:20; Matthew 26:23), where sharing the dish shows how close the betrayer was.

a: Know what your neighbor wants by what you want yourself
p: The KJV says 'Judge not thy neighbour by thyself', but the Greek has no 'not': judge him by yourself.
b: The Greek noei ta tou plēsion ek seautou means "understand your neighbor's things from yourself": think what he would like by what you would like. The KJV's "Judge not thy neighbour by thyself" adds a "not" and says the opposite. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition reads de'eh re'akha kenafshekha, "know your neighbor as yourself," a clear echo of "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). The verse is a form of the Golden Rule, applied to the dinner table (Tobit 4:15; Matthew 7:12).
orig: νόει τὰ τοῦ πλησίον ἐκ σεαυτοῦ (noei ta tou plēsion ek seautou)

a: Eat the food put in front of you
t: Eat what is set before you
p: Jesus tells his messengers the same: eat what is put in front of you.
b: The Greek ta parakeimena soi, "the things set before you," is close to Jesus' words to the seventy-two: "eat what they put in front of you" (Luke 10:8; Greek ta paratithemena hymin). Paul uses the same phrase for meals with unbelievers (1 Corinthians 10:27). Ben Sira's concern is manners; Jesus' is that his messengers not be fussy about food in the homes that welcome them.

a: out of good training
p: Paideia, here 'good training', is discipline or instruction elsewhere in this part.
b: Paideia is the upbringing a child receives: training, correction, education. In this part of Sirach the Plain renders it by context: "discipline" where correction is meant (30:33; 35:14), "instruction" where it is learning (30:26; 36:4), and here "good training," the manners of a well-brought-up guest. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has musar, the word rendered "discipline" in Proverbs. Compare "a well-trained person" (pepaideumenos) in 34:19.

a: nausea
p: The Greek word is cholera, a sickness of the bile; it is not the modern disease.
b: The word here is cholera, from cholē, "bile." Greek doctors used it for an attack of vomiting and diarrhea, which they blamed on bile, the sort of thing that follows a heavy meal. The English name of the modern disease comes from it, but Ben Sira means an upset stomach, not an epidemic. Strophos is colic, the twisting pain of the gut.

a: get up while the meal is going on and step away
p: The Greek says get up in the middle and step away; the Latin and the KJV say 'vomit'.
b: The Greek anasta mesoporōn means "get up, going away in the middle": leave the table and walk it off. The Latin reads surge e medio, evome, "get up from the middle, vomit," and the KJV follows: "arise, go forth, vomit." Greek and Roman diners sometimes made themselves sick to keep eating, but that is not what the Greek here says. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition is unclear at this point.

a: my child
p: The Greek says 'child', where the Hebrew has 'my son'.
b: The Greek teknon is "child," and the Plain writes "my child," as in the rest of Sirach. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has beni, "my son," the address of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:8). Ben Sira taught young men (51:23), so "my son" was what he said; the grandson's "child" is warmer and opens the advice to any reader.

a: In all your work be quick and skillful
p: Hard work keeps sickness away: practical advice, or a moral law?
b: Entrechēs means quick, skillful, nimble. Ben Sira joins diligence to health, as he joined moderate eating to sound sleep (34:20). Some readers take it as practical observation (busy people eat less and sleep better); others see the book's wider belief that wise living brings health, a belief Job and Ecclesiastes test (Job 2:7; Ecclesiastes 9:11). The next chapters return to health with the physician (38:1–15).

a: Do not play the hero over wine
p: Isaiah mocks the 'strongmen at drinking wine'.
b: The verb andrizou means "act the man, show your manhood." Isaiah: "Woe to the strongmen at drinking wine, / the warriors at mixing beer" (Isaiah 5:22). Proverbs: "Wine is a mocker, and beer is a rowdy" (Proverbs 20:1), and the long warning of Proverbs 23:29–35. Ben Sira's teaching on wine is balanced: wine was made for gladness (34:27), but drunkenness ruins (34:29–30).

a: As the furnace tests a steel edge in the tempering
p: A smith tests hardened iron by heating and plunging it; wine tests a man the same way.
b: The stomōma is the hardened edge of an iron blade; baphē is the "dipping" in water that tempers it after the furnace. The smith learns what the metal is made of. Wine does the same to the proud at a party: it shows what is in their hearts. The Bible often uses the furnace for testing (Proverbs 17:3; Isaiah 48:10).

a: Wine is as good as life to people
p: Ben Sira praises wine in measure, as the Psalms do; he warns against drunkenness, as Proverbs and Paul do.
b: Agrees. Wine is God's gift "that makes people glad at heart" (Psalm 104:15), "which cheers gods and humans" (Judges 9:13), and Ecclesiastes says "with a good heart drink your wine" (Ecclesiastes 9:7). Jesus made wine at a wedding (John 2:1–11) and Paul told Timothy to "take a little wine" (1 Timothy 5:23). The Bible also warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 23:29–35; Ephesians 5:18). Christian traditions differ in practice, from those that use wine at the Lord's Supper to Methodist, Baptist and other churches that have long urged abstinence; Ben Sira's line, "in its proper measure," is the middle path most of them accept in principle.
r: Psalm 104:15; Judges 9:13; Ecclesiastes 9:7; John 2:1–11; 1 Timothy 5:23; Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35

a: demanding what he owes you
p: The KJV says 'urging him to drink'; the Greek means pressing him to pay a debt.
b: Apaitēsis is a demand for repayment, from apaiteō, to ask back, the verb of Luke 6:30 ("do not ask for them back"). Ben Sira says: do not spoil a man's evening at a party by dunning him for what he owes. The Latin non premas illum repetendo, "do not press him by asking again," says the same. The KJV's "urging him to drink" is a guess from the setting, not the Greek.

a: Have they made you the leader of the feast?
p: Greek banquets chose a leader to run the evening; John 2 has one at the wedding at Cana.
b: In the Greek symposium, the drinking party after dinner, the guests chose one of themselves to lead: he set how strong the wine was mixed and kept order. Jews of the upper classes in Ben Sira's Jerusalem had taken up the custom, wreaths and music included (35:2–6). The hēgoumenos here is such a leader; John's Gospel calls the man in charge at Cana the architriklinos (John 2:8–9), and the site's note there points to this verse. A marginal hand in Vaticanus adds the heading "about leaders." Ben Sira's advice is humility: be one of the guests and look after them first (Luke 22:26).

a: win a wreath for keeping good order
p: Guests at Greek banquets wore wreaths; a good leader of the feast earned one as an honor.
b: At Greek parties guests wore wreaths of flowers or leaves, and a crown could also be an honor for service. Wisdom of Solomon has the ungodly say, "Let's wear crowns of rosebuds before they wilt" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:8). Ben Sira does not mind the custom; he wants the leader to earn his wreath by service. Paul contrasts such fading wreaths with the crown that does not fade (1 Corinthians 9:25).

a: do not get in the way of the music
p: Musicians played at banquets; Ben Sira tells the older guests not to talk over them.
b: Mousika is music, and the akroama of 35:4 is a performance to listen to. Rich Jews, like Greeks, hired musicians for their banquets. Isaiah and Amos condemn feasts with harp and wine where God is forgotten (Isaiah 5:12; Amos 6:5–6); Ben Sira praises music as a jewel (35:5–6) but ends with thanks to the God who gives all of it (35:13).

a: a seal of red gemstone
p: Anthrax is a glowing red stone, perhaps a garnet; smaragdos is an emerald or another green stone.
b: Anthrax, "coal," is a red stone that glows like a live coal, the KJV's "carbuncle," most likely a garnet. Smaragdos (35:6) is a green stone, the emerald or something like it. Both stand on the high priest's breastpiece in the Greek of Exodus 28:17–18, and the emerald is the rainbow's color in Revelation 4:3. A seal stone set in a gold ring was a rich man's treasure; good music at a banquet is that kind of jewel.

a: much in a few words
p: Proverbs and James give the same advice: few words, quick ears.
b: "With many words, wrongdoing does not stop; / the one who keeps his lips in check has good sense" (Proverbs 10:19). "Even a stubborn fool, if he stays silent, is counted as wise" (Proverbs 17:28). James: "let every person be ready to listen, slow to talk" (James 1:19). Ben Sira's advice to the young man at the banquet is the same: be brief, and know more than you say.

a: who fills you to the brim with his good things
p: The verb methyskō means 'make drunk'; here it is the overflowing of God's gifts.
b: Methyskonta se is literally "making you drunk." The Greek of Psalm 23:5 (22:5 in the Septuagint) uses the same verb for God's cup, "your cup, making drunk, like the best" (Hebrew: "my cup is brimming"). Ben Sira ends the banquet with a blessing to the Maker: the Law says, "When you have eaten and are full, bless the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 8:10), the root of the Jewish grace after meals.

a: those up at dawn
p: Rising early for God means seeking him eagerly, as Wisdom says in Proverbs 8:17.
b: The verb orthrizō means to rise at dawn. In the Psalms and Proverbs rising early is a picture of eager seeking: Wisdom says, "those who hunt hard for me will find me" (Proverbs 8:17), using the Hebrew verb of looking for something at dawn. The Hebrew of Ben Sira in Kahana's edition says "those who seek him early will find an answer." The Greek reads "will find favor." Swete's text spells the first word paidian, "play," a spelling slip for paideian, "discipline" (see the variant).

a: the hypocrite
p: The Greek word is the stage actor's word; the Hebrew speaks of one who toys with the law.
b: Ho hypokrinomenos is "the one who plays a part," from the word for a stage actor, the root of "hypocrite" (Matthew 6:2). In the Greek of Ben Sira it marks the man who only pretends to keep the law (36:2). The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has mitlahleah, "one who toys with it, acts like a madman," the word Proverbs 26:18 uses for a madman shooting flaming arrows. So the law fills the seeker but is a snare to the one who plays games with it.

a: the stranger and the proud man
p: The Greek says 'the stranger'; the Hebrew has zed, 'arrogant', which looks very like zar, 'stranger'.
b: The Greek allotrios means "foreign, a stranger." The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has zed, "arrogant" ("the arrogant and the mocker will not keep the law"). In Hebrew script the letters d (ד) and r (ר) look nearly the same, and zar means "stranger." It is likely that the grandson read or had a copy with zar. Either way the contrast is with the man of counsel: the proud man acts on his own and is not afraid.

a: Do nothing without counsel
p: Proverbs and Tobit urge the same: plans succeed with good advice.
b: "Without someone to talk them over, plans break down; / with plenty of advisers, they hold" (Proverbs 15:22). Tobit tells his son, "Ask every sensible person for advice" (Tobit 4:18). Ben Sira adds the other side: once you have taken counsel and acted, do not torment yourself with regret. Chapter 37 returns to choosing counselors.

a: watch out for your own children
p: The Greek says 'beware of your children'; the Hebrew says 'be careful in your paths'.
b: The Greek apo tōn teknōn sou phylaxai means "guard yourself from your children," a strange line after two lines about roads. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has "be careful in your paths" and, in a second form of the line, "guard your end." The Hebrew word for "end," acharit, can also mean "what comes after you," your descendants (as in Psalm 109:13, "Let what comes after him be cut down"). The grandson may have read it that way. See the variant.
orig: ἀπὸ τῶν τέκνων σου φύλαξαι (apo tōn teknōn sou phylaxai)

a: trust yourself
p: The Greek says 'trust your soul'; the Hebrew says 'guard your soul'.
b: The Greek pisteue tē psychē sou is "trust your soul," have confidence in yourself, which sits oddly beside the warnings of 35:20–22. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition reads shemor nafshekha, "guard yourself," and gives the reason, "for whoever does this keeps the commandment." Proverbs says, "More than anything you keep watch over, watch over your heart" (Proverbs 4:23). See the variant.
orig: πίστευε τῇ ψυχῇ σου (pisteue tē psychē sou)

a: Whoever trusts the law pays attention to the commandments
t: Trusting the law and trusting the Lord
p: Ben Sira puts trust in the law beside trust in the Lord.
b: The two lines stand side by side: trusting the law and relying on the Lord go together. For Ben Sira the law is the form God's wisdom takes in Israel (24:23), so to trust it is to trust God. Jewish readers have found here the heart of a life lived by Torah. Paul argues that the law cannot give life by itself (Galatians 3:21) while still calling it "holy" (Romans 7:12); Christian traditions differ on how the law relates to grace. In the Hebrew in Kahana's edition the second line reads "whoever trusts in the LORD will not be put to shame."

a: is tossed like a ship in a squall
p: James uses a sea picture for the double-minded.
b: The one who only plays at the law has nothing steady under him. James says the doubter "is like an ocean wave that the wind whips up and throws about" and "never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:6–8). Ephesians 4:14 speaks of being "tossed" by every wind of teaching. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition begins differently: "One who hates the law will not become wise."

a: an inquiry made by the righteous
t: Inquiry of the righteous, or of the Urim?
p: Vaticanus reads 'of the righteous'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read 'of the Urim'; the Hebrew says 'like the Urim in the breastpiece'.
b: An erōtēma is a question put to God for an answer, an oracle. Swete's text (B) reads dikaiōn, "of the righteous." Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read dēlōn, the Septuagint's word for the Urim, the high priest's lots for asking God's decision (Numbers 27:21; Deuteronomy 33:8 in Greek). The Hebrew in Kahana's edition is plain: "his law is like the Urim in the breastpiece," the pouch over the high priest's heart that held them (Exodus 28:30). So the original thought is: for the wise man the law is as sure as the Urim once were. 1 Esdras calls the Urim and Thummim "the Showing and the Truth" (1 Esdras 5:40). See the variant.

a: A stallion kept for breeding
p: A false friend is like a stallion that neighs at every rider; Jeremiah uses the stallion for lust.
b: The hippos eis ocheian is a stud horse, kept for mating. It neighs under any rider, as a mocking friend fawns on everyone and is loyal to none. Jeremiah uses the stallion for faithless Israel: "They are stallions, fed up and full of lust, / each one neighing at his neighbor's wife" (Jeremiah 5:8). A corrector of Sinaiticus reads "a foolish friend" (mōros) for "a mocking friend."

a: Why is one day above another
p: Why are some days holy? Ben Sira answers from creation; Paul uses the same words about the Sabbath and feasts.
b: All days get their light from the same sun, so why are some holy (the Sabbath, the feasts) and others ordinary? Ben Sira answers: because the Lord set them apart in his wisdom (36:8–9), as he blessed the seventh day (Genesis 2:3) and made the lights that "will mark the appointed times" (Genesis 1:14). Paul uses similar words for a debate in the church at Rome: "One person judges one day to stand above another, and another judges every day alike" (Romans 14:5). Christians differ on whether the Sabbath or holy days still bind; see the topic on the Sabbath.
r: Genesis 1:14; Genesis 2:3; Leviticus 23:1–4; Romans 14:5–6; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16

a: Adam was made out of earth
p: Ben Sira moves from days to people: all come from the same earth, yet God chose some.
b: "The LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7); "you were taken from it" (Genesis 3:19). This is the first mention of Adam by name in this part of the book (compare 17:1; 49:16). The argument: as days are alike in their light yet God made some holy, so people are alike in their clay, yet God chose some and set others aside (36:11–12).

a: Some he blessed and lifted up
t: Whom did God bless and curse?
p: Israel and the priests blessed and brought near; the Canaanites cursed and turned out of their place.
b: Most interpreters read the verse from Israel's story. Those God blessed and lifted up are Abraham's family and Israel (Genesis 12:2); those he made holy and brought near are the priests and Levites (Numbers 16:5, "He will bring that one near to himself"); those he cursed and threw down from their place are the Canaanites (Genesis 9:25), driven out before Israel. Others read it more broadly, of all humanity, divided by God into the godly and the sinners (36:14). Ben Sira does not settle the question of free will here; he had said at 15:14 that God left humanity in the hand of its own choice. The card on free will in chapter 15 sets out how churches read those verses.

a: As clay is in the potter's hand
p: Jeremiah, Isaiah, Wisdom and Paul use the potter picture; here it supports God's choosing.
b: Jeremiah: "Look, as clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel" (Jeremiah 18:6). Isaiah: "Does the clay say to the one who shapes it, 'What are you making?'" (Isaiah 45:9; compare Isaiah 64:8). Wisdom of Solomon shows a potter making, from the same clay, pots for clean uses "and those for the opposite" (Wisdom of Solomon 15:7). Paul: "From one lump of clay, does the potter not have the authority to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" (Romans 9:21). Ben Sira is close to Paul: God gives each person a place "as he judges." In Jeremiah the clay can be reworked if the nation turns (Jeremiah 18:8); Ben Sira's verse is silent on that, but the book insists elsewhere on human choice (15:14–17).
r: Jeremiah 18:1–10; Isaiah 45:9; Isaiah 64:8; Isaiah 29:16; Wisdom of Solomon 15:7; Romans 9:20–21; 15:14–17

a: they come two by two, one across from the other
p: Ben Sira sees creation in pairs of opposites, good and evil, life and death.
b: Ben Sira teaches that God made everything in pairs, "two by two, one across from the other" (compare 42:24). Good has evil as its opposite, life has death, the godly have the sinner. Ecclesiastes says something like it: "God made this one to match that one" (Ecclesiastes 7:14), and the Ecclesiastes notes on this site point here. Some scholars compare Greek Stoic ideas of opposites in the world's order; others the Jewish teaching of the two ways ("life and what is good, death and what is bad," Deuteronomy 30:15). Ben Sira's point is that even the existence of sinners has a place in God's design, without God being the cause of sin (15:11–13).

a: I too kept watch, the last of all
p: This verse joins two half-lines from far apart: KJV 33:16a and KJV 36:11b.
b: In the Greek manuscripts this verse is where the two swapped blocks meet. Its first half, "I too kept watch, the last of all," is KJV 33:16a and belongs before the gleaner of 30:25. Its second half, "and you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning," is KJV 36:11b and finishes the prayer's "Gather all the tribes of Jacob" (33:13). So 36:16 holds the end of a sentence from 30:25's block and the end of a sentence from 33:13's block, written as one line. From 36:17 on the Greek and the KJV agree again in content (36:17–31 = KJV 36:12–26). See the notes at 30:24 and 30:25.

a: you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning
t: The inheritance as at the beginning
p: The tribes, once gathered, are to receive their land again as when Joshua divided it.
b: The verb kataklēronomeō is used in the Greek of Joshua for dividing the land among the tribes. "As at the beginning" looks back to that first allotment. The prayer hopes for Israel's restoration in the land, the hope of the prophets (Ezekiel 47:13–14; Micah 7:14, "like the days long ago"). John 11:52's "to bring God's scattered children together into one" is often compared with this verse and 33:13.

a: Israel, whom you likened to a firstborn
p: God calls Israel 'my son, my firstborn'; the Hebrew here says 'whom you named firstborn'.
b: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22); "Ephraim is my firstborn" (Jeremiah 31:9). The Greek says God "likened" Israel to a firstborn; the Hebrew in Kahana's edition says "whom you named firstborn." The firstborn had the first claim on a father's love and inheritance. The New Testament calls Christ "the firstborn among many brothers" (Romans 8:29) and the church "the assembly of the firstborn" (Hebrews 12:23).

a: a people that bears your name
p: To be called by God's name is to belong to him.
b: The Greek keklēmenon ep' onomati sou, "called by your name," is the Bible's way of saying God owns a people or a place: "my people, over whom my name has been called" (2 Chronicles 7:14); "your name is called over your city and your people" (Daniel 9:19). The priestly blessing puts God's name on Israel (Numbers 6:27), which the prayer recalls in 36:22.

a: Jerusalem, the city of your rest
p: Psalm 132 calls Zion God's resting place.
b: "This is my place of rest forever and ever. / Here I will make my home" (Psalm 132:14). In Ben Sira's time the temple had been rebuilt and repaired; he praises the high priest Simon who fortified it (50:1–4). The Hebrew in Kahana's edition says "the place where you dwell."

a: raise up the prophecies that bear your name
p: The prayer asks God to bring about what the prophets foretold, at a time when prophecy seemed silent.
b: Ben Sira asks God to "raise up" (bring to pass) the prophecies spoken in his name and to prove his prophets trustworthy (36:21). Many readers hear the sense, found also in Psalm 74:9 ("There is no prophet now") and 1 Maccabees ("until a prophet should come," 1 Maccabees 4:46), that the age of prophecy was over and Israel waited for its promises. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition reads "raise up the vision spoken in your name." "Those you made at the beginning" is most likely Israel, the first of God's works in Ben Sira's eyes (the Hebrew says "the first of your works"). Christians read the New Testament's "so that what the Lord spoke through the prophet would be fulfilled" (Matthew 1:22) as the answer.

a: as Aaron blessed your people
p: The Greek asks God to hear according to the priestly blessing; the Hebrew says 'according to your good will'.
b: The priestly blessing that Aaron and his sons spoke over Israel, "May the LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24–26), is God's promise to bless those who bear his name (Numbers 6:27). The Greek asks God to answer the prayer as that blessing promised. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition reads instead "according to your good will toward your people" (see the variant). Ben Sira will describe the high priest Simon giving the blessing in the temple (50:20–21).

a: God of all the ages
p: Ho theos tōn aiōnōn, 'God of the ages', is the Hebrew 'God of eternity'.
b: The Greek ho theos tōn aiōnōn renders the Hebrew El olam, "God of eternity" (the Hebrew in Kahana's edition has Elohei olam), the name Abraham calls on at Beersheba (Genesis 21:33). Paul's "the King of the ages" (1 Timothy 1:17) is close to it.
orig: ὁ θεὸς τῶν αἰώνων (ho theos tōn aiōnōn)

a: so a discerning heart tastes lies
p: Job says the ear tests words as the palate tastes food.
b: "The ear puts words to the test, does it not, / just as the mouth tastes food to eat?" (Job 12:11). Ben Sira turns it into a proverb: a wise heart can tell lies as the tongue tells one meat from another. It leads into choosing a wife (36:26): a man must taste and choose with care.

a: A woman will accept any male
t: Compared with the Bible: who chooses in marriage
p: Ben Sira assumes a daughter takes whatever husband she is given; the man chooses.
b: The verse reflects marriage in Ben Sira's world: a father gave his daughter in marriage, and she had little say (compare 7:25), while a man could pick among daughters. The Bible shows both customs. Rebekah is asked whether she will go (Genesis 24:57–58), Laban gives his daughters as he pleases (Genesis 29:23–28), and Paul says a widow is free to marry "the man she chooses, but only in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:39). Agrees with the Bible's picture of the ancient practice; it does not state a command. Readers in every tradition today take it as a description of its time. The second half of the Hebrew line in Kahana's edition is his own restoration, so it is not cited here.

a: If there is mercy and gentleness on her tongue
p: The woman of strength in Proverbs has 'the teaching of loyal love' on her tongue.
b: "When she opens her mouth, it is with wisdom, / and on her tongue is the teaching of loyal love" (Proverbs 31:26). Eleos, "mercy," is the Septuagint's usual word for hesed, "loyal love." Ben Sira, who often warns against a bad wife (25:16–26), praises a kind one: her husband is luckier than other men.

a: a helper who is his match
t: A helper who is his match
p: The Greek words are those of Genesis 2:18 in the Septuagint.
b: Boēthon kat' auton is the exact Greek of Genesis 2:18 in the Septuagint: "I will make him a helper who is his match." Ben Sira reads marriage through the creation story. The Hebrew in Kahana's edition has "a helper and a fortress and a pillar to lean on." Proverbs agrees that a good wife is a gift: "The one who finds a wife has found something good" (Proverbs 18:22); "a wife with good sense comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 19:14). The verb "gets" (ktōmenos, "acquires") reflects the bride-price custom, in which the groom's family paid the bride's.

a: a man wanders about groaning
p: The Hebrew uses Cain's words, 'a homeless wanderer'; the Greek 'groaning' matches the Septuagint of Cain too.
b: The Hebrew in Kahana's edition says a man without a wife is na' wanad, a wanderer and a drifter, the very words God speaks to Cain: "You will be a homeless wanderer on the earth" (Genesis 4:12). The Greek of Genesis 4:12 has Cain "groaning and trembling" (stenōn kai tremōn), and the grandson here writes "he will groan, wandering" (stenaxei planōmenos). Both languages tie the unmarried man to Cain. The "fence" of the first line is a vineyard's hedge in the Hebrew.
orig: στενάξει πλανώμενος (stenaxei planōmenos); Hebrew נָע וָנָד (na' wanad)

a: a man who has no nest of his own
t: Claude's theory: the Son of Man with no nest
p: Ben Sira's homeless, unmarried man is the opposite of his ideal; Jesus chose that life.
b: This is Claude's own observation, not a published claim I know of. Ben Sira ends his praise of marriage with a warning: no one trusts a man with no nest who lodges wherever night finds him (36:30–31). Jesus says of himself, "Foxes have their holes, and the birds in the sky have places to roost, but the Son of Man does not have anywhere to rest his head" (Luke 9:58). He was unmarried and went from town to town (Luke 8:1), the very figure Ben Sira's readers would distrust. Whether Luke's readers heard the contrast cannot be shown; the point is that Jesus deliberately took a path that the respected wisdom of his people called untrustworthy, and asked his disciples to do the same (Luke 9:57–62; Matthew 19:12).
